etymology: Hebrew Shachatsimah, perhaps “heights” or “lofty places”; a town of Issachar near Tabor, on the border reaching to Jordan.
biblical_def: Shahazimah was a town of Issachar, named as the tribal coast ran toward Tabor and the Jordan: “And the coast reacheth to Tabor, and Shahazimah, and Bethshemesh; and the outgoings of their border were at Jordan” (Josh 19:22). Issachar lay in the good and pleasant vale of Jezreel, between the hills of Galilee and the ridge of Carmel, a fertile plain that made the tribe a willing labourer. Jacob had seen it: “Issachar is a strong ass couching down between two burdens: and he saw that rest was good, and the land that it was pleasant; and bowed his shoulder to bear” (Gen 49:14-15). Shahazimah, if its name means “heights,” stood among the swelling grounds of that rich plain. The tribe of the strong ass preaches the dignity of patient labour and the danger of ease. Issachar bore his burden willingly, and Moses blessed him to rejoice in his tents; yet the love of ease that bowed the shoulder to tribute could sink into servility if rest were prized above righteousness. The believer learns to labour gladly and bear his burden, taking the yoke of Christ, which is easy, and finding rest not in the pleasantness of the land but in the God who gives His beloved rest.

etymology: Hebrew Ebets, of uncertain meaning, perhaps “lofty” or “white”; a town of Issachar, named once.
biblical_def: Abez was a town of Issachar, listed once with Rabbith and Kishion: “And Rabbith, and Kishion, and Abez” (Josh 19:20). Nothing of its history survives; it is a name in the roll of the tribe’s inheritance and no more. It lay in the portion of Issachar, the labouring tribe of the vale of Jezreel, whom Moses blessed together with Zebulun: “Rejoice, Zebulun, in thy going out; and, Issachar, in thy tents” (Deu 33:18). While Zebulun went out to the sea and to trade, Issachar rejoiced at home in his tents and his tilled fields. Abez, an obscure town of the home-keeping tribe, preaches the quiet blessedness of faithful ordinary life. Not all are called to go out to great ventures; many are called, like Issachar, to rejoice in their tents, to keep the home, till the ground, raise the children, and serve God in the round of common days. The men of Issachar were known as those who had understanding of the times, to know what Israel ought to do. Wisdom and blessing are not reserved for the conspicuous; the obscure town of a home-keeping tribe reminds us that God is honoured in the faithful discharge of humble, settled duty as much as in the boldest going-out.

etymology: Hebrew Yidalah, of uncertain meaning; a town of Zebulun near Bethlehem of Galilee, named once.
biblical_def: Idalah was a town of Zebulun, listed among the tribe’s cities near the little Bethlehem of Galilee: “And Kattath, and Nahallal, and Shimron, and Idalah, and Bethlehem: twelve cities with their villages” (Josh 19:15). Zebulun lay in the north, toward the sea and the trading routes, of whom Jacob prophesied, “Zebulun shall dwell at the haven of the sea; and he shall be for an haven of ships” (Gen 49:13), and Moses said, “Rejoice, Zebulun, in thy going out” (Deu 33:18). Idalah, an obscure town of that seafaring tribe, shares in a striking honour: it lay in the country of Galilee where, centuries later, the Light would dawn. For the LORD who lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and Naphtali would afterward more gloriously honour it; the people that walked in darkness saw a great light, and Galilee of the nations beheld the rising of the Sun of righteousness. The Lord Jesus was reared in Nazareth, in the old land of Zebulun, and there began His ministry. Idalah, a nameless town of the tribe of the sea-haven, reminds us that God delights to bring His greatest glory to the obscure and the despised, and that the light which the world overlooks may rise first upon the forgotten places.

etymology: Hebrew Dimnah, perhaps “dung-heap” or “place of manure”; a Levitical city of Zebulun given to the Merarite Levites; called Rimmono in the parallel list.
biblical_def: Dimnah was a Levitical city in the tribe of Zebulun, given with its suburbs to the Levites of the family of Merari: “Dimnah with her suburbs, Nahalal with her suburbs; four cities” (Josh 21:35). In the parallel account it appears as Rimmono. Its name, perhaps “dung-heap,” is lowly and even unlovely, yet this was a city set apart for the servants of God’s house. Therein lies its quiet sermon: God takes the base and lowly things and consecrates them to holy use. The Levites had no inheritance of their own, but were scattered through the tribes in such cities, that the law and the worship of the LORD might be near all the people. That a city with so mean a name should be a holy city of the Levites preaches the grace that dignifies the lowly. God chooses the base things of the world, and things which are despised, and things which are not, to bring to nought the things that are, that no flesh should glory in His presence. The dung-hill is lifted, the beggar set among princes; and the sinner, base and defiled, is washed, sanctified, and made a dwelling-place for the Spirit of God. Dimnah, a Levite city of the humble name, is a token of that transforming grace.

etymology: Hebrew Neah, perhaps “a shaking” or “movement”; a town on the border of Zebulun, named once.
biblical_def: Neah was a landmark on the eastern border of Zebulun, named as the line ran its course: the border “passeth on along on the east to Gittahhepher, to Ittahkazin, and goeth out to Remmonmethoar to Neah” (Josh 19:13). It is one of the many boundary points by which the inheritance of Zebulun was measured, the tribe of whom Jacob said he should be a haven of ships and Moses bade him rejoice in his going out (Gen 49:13). Nothing more of Neah is known; it marks a turning of the line and no more. Yet even a turning-point in a border serves the purpose of God, for by these lines He fixed the dwelling of His people, that each tribe might know its own and dwell in peace beside its brethren. Zebulun and Naphtali were tribes that jeoparded their lives unto the death in the high places of the field (Judg 5:18); they were valiant in Israel’s wars. Neah, a nameless corner of Zebulun’s border, preaches that the boundaries God appoints are not arbitrary lines but the wise gift of a Father who sets every one of His children in the place He has chosen, and calls each to be faithful and valiant in his own appointed portion.

etymology: Hebrew Yaphia, “shining” or “bright”; a town on the border of Zebulun; distinct from the persons of the same name.
biblical_def: Japhia was a town on the border of Zebulun, named as the line turned eastward: “And turned from Sarid eastward toward the sunrising unto the border of Chislothtabor, and then goeth out to Daberath, and goeth up to Japhia” (Josh 19:12). This is a place, distinct from Japhia king of Lachish whom Joshua overthrew, and from Japhia a son of David born in Jerusalem. The name means “shining” or “bright,” and it belonged to Zebulun, the tribe of the land of Galilee where the great Light would one day shine. Set toward the sunrising, a town called “shining” is a fitting emblem of the dawn. For upon the land of Zebulun and Naphtali the Sun of righteousness arose with healing in His wings; the people that sat in darkness saw a great light. Japhia, a bright town of the tribe of the sea-haven, preaches that the children of God are called to shine. They are the light of the world, a city set on a hill; they are to let their light so shine before men that others may see their good works and glorify the Father. The brightness is not their own but the reflected glory of Christ, the true and rising Sun, in whose light they shine as lights in a dark world.

etymology: Hebrew Cheleph, “exchange” or “passing”; the starting-point of the border of Naphtali, near the oak in Zaanannim.
biblical_def: Heleph was the starting-point of the border of Naphtali, named at the head of the tribe’s boundary: “And their coast was from Heleph, from Allon to Zaanannim, and Adami, Nekeb, and Jabneel, unto Lakum; and the outgoings thereof were at Jordan” (Josh 19:33). Naphtali lay in the fair north of Galilee, of whom Jacob said, “Naphtali is a hind let loose: he giveth goodly words” (Gen 49:21), and Moses, “O Naphtali, satisfied with favour, and full with the blessing of the LORD” (Deu 33:23). Heleph, whose name means “exchange” or “passing,” stood where the line began its course toward Jordan. It preaches the passing nature of every earthly bound and the abiding favour of God. Borders shift and possessions change hands; Naphtali’s land was later among the first carried into captivity. But the tribe blessed as “satisfied with favour” teaches that the true and unchanging inheritance is the favour and blessing of the LORD, which no exchange can take away. The believer, though his earthly bounds pass and his possessions fail, is satisfied with favour and full of the blessing of God, and holds an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven.

etymology: Hebrew Adami ha-Neqeb, “Adami of the pass” (the earth of the pass); a place on the border of Naphtali, named once.
biblical_def: Adami-nekeb was a place on the border of Naphtali, named in the tracing of the tribal line: the coast ran “from Allon to Zaanannim, and Adami, Nekeb, and Jabneel, unto Lakum” (Josh 19:33). The name joins Adami, from the word for earth or red ground, with Nekeb, a pass or defile; it is “the earth of the pass,” a settlement guarding a way through the hills of Galilee. The word adam, earth or ground, is the very root of the name of the first man, formed of the dust of the ground, and reminds us of the frailty of all flesh: dust we are, and unto dust we shall return. A town named for the red earth at a mountain pass preaches the humility that becomes the sons of Adam. We are of the earth, earthy; our days are as grass; the wind passeth over the flower of the field and it is gone. Yet the God who formed man of the dust breathed into him the breath of life, and the second Adam, the Lord from heaven, raises His people from the dust to bear the image of the heavenly. Adami-nekeb, the earth of the pass, bids us walk humbly, remembering our dust, and hope in the God who quickens the dead.

etymology: Hebrew Aznoth Tabor, “the ears (or peaks) of Tabor”; a place on the border of Naphtali near Mount Tabor.
biblical_def: Aznoth-tabor, “the ears of Tabor,” was a place on the border of Naphtali near the great rounded height of Mount Tabor: the coast “turneth westward to Aznothtabor, and goeth out from thence to Hukkok” (Josh 19:34). The name likely marks the summits or shoulders — the “ears” — of Tabor, that noble mountain standing up alone above the plain of Jezreel. Tabor was a place of gathering and of victory: there Barak, at Deborah’s word, gathered ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun and came down to rout Sisera, and Zebulun and Naphtali were a people that jeoparded their lives unto the death in the high places of the field (Judg 5:18). Aznoth-tabor, on the flank of that mountain, preaches the readiness of faith to gather at God’s call and go down to battle. The tribes did not shrink when the LORD summoned them by His prophetess, but hazarded their lives and won a great deliverance. So the people of God are called to muster at His word, to count not their lives dear, and to come down from the mountain of prayer into the field of conflict, assured that the LORD who called Barak from Tabor goes before His people to give the victory.

So the people of God muster at His word, count not their lives dear, and come down from the mountain of prayer into the field of conflict, assured that the LORD goes before them to give the victory.

etymology: Hebrew Chuqqoq, “appointed” or “decreed” (from the root for a statute or decree); a place on the border of Naphtali, named once.
biblical_def: Hukkok was a place on the western border of Naphtali, named as the line ran its course: the coast turned to Aznoth-tabor, “and goeth out from thence to Hukkok, and reacheth to Zebulun on the south side” (Josh 19:34). Its name comes from the root that gives the Hebrew words for a statute, an ordinance, a thing decreed and engraven — “appointed” or “marked out.” It is a fitting name for a boundary-point, for the borders of the tribes were not drawn by chance but appointed and decreed by the LORD, who fixed the bounds of His people. The name preaches the great comfort of the divine decree. What God has appointed stands sure; His counsel shall stand, and He will do all His pleasure. The bounds of every man’s dwelling and the number of his days are appointed of God, engraven in His book, and none can pass the bound He has set. This is no cold fate but the loving decree of a Father, who has appointed His people to salvation, appointed them their portion, and appointed a kingdom for them as His Father appointed unto Him. Hukkok, the “appointed” town of Naphtali’s border, bids the believer rest in the unchangeable decree of the God who works all things after the counsel of His own will.
